title: Intensive Blood-Pressure Lowering in Patients with Type 2 Diabetes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Whether a systolic blood-pressure (SBP) target below 120 mm Hg reduces cardiovascular events in patients with type 2 diabetes remains contested: ACCORD-BP was neutral whereas the more recent BPROAD trial in China was positive. OPTIMAL-DIABETES (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT04040634) was designed to test an intensive target in an ethnically diverse, high-cardiovascular-risk diabetic population. METHODS: OPTIMAL-DIABETES was a multicenter, randomized, open-label trial conducted in Brazil. Eligible patients were adults (reported as 50 years of age or older) with elevated blood pressure, type 2 diabetes and high cardiovascular risk, defined by established cardiovascular disease, subclinical cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease or other cardiovascular risk factors. Patients were randomly assigned to intensive therapy targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg or to standard therapy targeting an SBP of less than 140 mm Hg. The primary outcome was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for unstable angina or heart failure. Of 9,476 patients enrolled, 4,745 were assigned to intensive therapy and 4,731 to standard therapy. RESULTS: Mean SBP during follow-up was approximately 122 mm Hg in the intensive-therapy group and approximately 135 mm Hg in the standard-therapy group. Over a median follow-up of 4.0 years, the primary composite outcome occurred in 6.0% of patients in the intensive-therapy group and in 6.7% of patients in the standard-therapy group (hazard ratio, 0.90; P=0.20); the 95% confidence interval for this hazard ratio could not be confirmed by two independent sources and is therefore not reported here. The difference was not statistically significant. Rates of serious adverse events were similar in the two groups. Renal events were reported to be more frequent with intensive therapy, attributed mainly to a hemodynamic reduction in estimated glomerular filtration rate, although this was corroborated by only one source. CONCLUSIONS: Among patients with type 2 diabetes, elevated blood pressure and high cardiovascular risk, targeting an SBP of less than 120 mm Hg did not reduce the incidence of major cardiovascular events as compared with a target of less than 140 mm Hg. The investigators explicitly caution that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that more intensive blood-pressure lowering is ineffective in people with type 2 diabetes: they suggest that any cardiovascular benefit may be smaller in diabetes than in people without diabetes, such that a trial of this size may not have been able to detect a modest yet clinically meaningful effect.

title: Obesity, frail obesity, and outcomes after durable left ventricular assist device implantation: a pooled analysis of the MOMENTUM 3 trials
abstract: BACKGROUND AND AIMS: Obesity in patients supported by left ventricular assist devices (LVADs) is linked to excess mortality and haemocompatibility-related events. Whether this association persists with the fully magnetically levitated HeartMate 3 (HM3) pump is unknown. This analysis tested outcomes with obesity and the additive influence of co-existing frailty ('frail obesity') in the contemporary era. METHODS: The study pooled 2200 HM3 recipients from the MOMENTUM 3 pivotal randomized trial (n = 515) and Continued Access Protocol (n = 1685). Obesity was defined as body mass index (BMI) ≥30 kg/m2 and frailty by a 40-item Rockwood cumulative-deficit frailty index (FI), with clinically relevant frailty defined as FI ≥0.325 (moderate-severe frailty); BMI was excluded from the FI to avoid mathematical coupling. The primary endpoint was survival to transplant, recovery, or 24 months of support free of disabling stroke (modified Rankin score >3) or pump replacement reoperation. RESULTS: Obese patients (n = 887, 40.3%) were younger, less often with ischaemic aetiology, and more frequently women, but more often had diabetes and hypertension, than non-obese patients. Unadjusted 2-year outcomes were similar between groups (freedom from the primary endpoint: 75.1% vs 77.1%, log-rank P = .34; survival: 79.9% vs 81.2%, P = .57). After covariate adjustment, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of the primary endpoint (hazard ratio [HR] 1.30, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.07-1.58) and all-cause mortality (HR 1.35, 95% CI 1.10-1.67), as well as heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia, but not stroke, bleeding, or early right heart failure. Frailty affected 67.3% of obese recipients (571/849) and was associated with a higher adjusted risk of the primary endpoint (HR 1.51, 95% CI 1.09-2.10), overall mortality and non-haemocompatibilty-related morbidity endpoints. The obesity-by-frailty interaction was not significant for either the primary endpoint (P = .436) or mortality (P = .215), indicating additive rather than synergistic risk; frail-obese patients nonetheless carried the highest absolute risk of any subgroup. Frailty improved by at least one severity class by 6 months in 75.9% of frail-obese patients, and improvement was associated with better survival (adjusted HR 0.14, 95% CI 0.07-0.26). CONCLUSIONS: In the HM3 era, obese and non-obese recipients had similar unadjusted 2-year outcomes; however, after adjustment for baseline case-mix, obesity was independently associated with a higher risk of both the primary endpoint and all-cause mortality, together with heart failure hospitalization, infection, and arrhythmia. Frailty was independently associated with adverse outcomes across nearly all endpoints and was highly prevalent among obese recipients; the combination of obesity and frailty was additive but not synergistic, with frail-obese patients carrying the highest absolute risk. Frailty, however, proved substantially reversible after LVAD support, and its improvement was associated with markedly better survival. Obesity and frailty should therefore be assessed together, rather than through BMI thresholds alone, with recognition that frailty status is dynamic after implantation and that improvement in frailty is associated with markedly better survival.

title: Initial Diabetes Therapy After Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting and Long-Term Outcomes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes (T2D) is common among patients undergoing coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG), but optimal post-CABG glucose-lowering therapy remains uncertain. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using the OptumLabs Data Warehouse of adults with T2D undergoing isolated CABG from 2012-2024. Follow-up began 30 days after discharge. Glucose-lowering therapy was modeled as a time-varying exposure with patients contributing no-observed-therapy person-time until the first qualifying post-discharge fill. Pairwise comparisons used stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality; secondary outcomes were heart failure hospitalization, stroke, and repeat coronary revascularization. RESULTS: Among 19,237 patients, 24.9% had no observed post-discharge therapy, 42.8% received metformin, 22.9% received insulin, and 9.4% received GLP-1RA/SGLT2i therapy. All active therapies were associated with lower mortality compared with no observed therapy, including GLP-1RA/SGLT2i (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.58-0.87), metformin (HR 0.60, 95% CI 0.55-0.66), and insulin (HR 0.75, 95% CI 0.67-0.84). Among active therapies, metformin was associated with lower mortality than insulin (HR, 0.61 [0.54-0.70]); GLP-1RA/SGLT2i comparisons with metformin and insulin were less precise. Metformin was also associated with lower cumulative incidence of heart failure hospitalization than no observed therapy and insulin, and lower stroke incidence than insulin. CONCLUSIONS: Observed glucose-lowering therapy initiation after CABG was associated with lower mortality compared with no observed therapy across all active treatment groups. These findings highlight a potential care gap and suggest that proper initiation of diabetes therapy after CABG represents an important opportunity to improve long-term outcomes following surgical revascularization.

title: Statin-Ezetimibe Combination Therapy versus Statin Monotherapy in Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: A Prespecified Secondary Analysis of the Randomized Ez-PAVE Trial
abstract: BACKGROUND: In a target-directed low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C)-lowering strategy, the impact of the initial treatment regimen has not been investigated in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. We compared the efficacy and safety of initial statin-ezetimibe combination therapy versus statin monotherapy within intensive or conventional LDL-C-targeting strategies. METHODS: In this prespecified second randomization of the randomized Ez-PAVE trial (Effects of Ezetimibe Combination Therapy for Patients With Atherosclerotic Cardiovascular Disease: Randomized Comparison of LDL Cholesterol Targeting <70 versus <55 mg/dL) conducted at 17 centers in South Korea, a total of 3048 patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease were enrolled between January 2021 and July 2022. Following the first randomization to either an intensive (<55 mg/dL) or conventional (<70 mg/dL) LDL-C-targeting strategy, patients underwent subsequent randomization (initial statin-ezetimibe combination therapy [n=1525] versus statin monotherapy [n=1523]) and were followed up for 3 years. Lipid-lowering therapy was adjusted according to a predefined protocol to achieve LDL-C targets. The primary end point was a 3-year composite of death from cardiovascular causes, nonfatal myocardial infarction, nonfatal stroke, any revascularization, or hospitalization for unstable angina. RESULTS: The mean±SD age was 64.4±9.0 years, and 638 patients (20.9%) were female. The incidence of the primary end point did not differ between statin-ezetimibe combination therapy (128 patients [8.5%]) and statin monotherapy (119 patients [7.9%]; hazard ratio, 1.07 [95% CI, 0.83-1.37]; P=0.596). Patients who received statin-ezetimibe combination therapy achieved lower median LDL-C levels during follow-up than those who received statin monotherapy in both the intensive-targeting (53 mg/dL [interquartile range, 45-62 mg/dL] versus 62 mg/dL [interquartile range, 53-74 mg/dL]) and conventional-targeting (63 mg/dL [interquartile range, 55-73 mg/dL] versus 70 mg/dL [interquartile range, 62-81 mg/dL]) strategies. During follow-up, ezetimibe was added to the treatment regimen of 241 patients (34.3%) and 177 patients (24.8%) who initially received statin monotherapy in the intensive- and conventional-targeting strategies, respectively. The treatment effect of intensive-targeting versus conventional-targeting strategies was consistent regardless of therapy regimens without significant heterogeneity (Pinteraction=0.583). The safety end points were similar between the groups. CONCLUSIONS: Within a target-directed LDL-C-lowering strategy, cardiovascular efficacy and safety did not differ significantly, whether initiated as statin-ezetimibe combination therapy or as statin monotherapy, but combination therapy facilitated achievement of a lower LDL-C target. REGISTRATION: URL: https://www.clinicaltrials.gov; Unique identifier: NCT04626973.

title: Prevalence, clinical implications and prognostic impact of frailty and other geriatric conditions in patients with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy
abstract: INTRODUCTION AND OBJECTIVES: Frailty in transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) remains poorly characterized. The aim of this study was to analyze the prevalence and prognostic influence of frailty and other geriatric conditions such as nutritional risk, cognitive status, depression, and dependence in patients with ATTR-CM. METHODS: We performed an observational, prospective, single-center study of 110 ATTR-CM patients who underwent comprehensive geriatric assessment from October 2024 to April 2025 and were followed up to September 2026. Study endpoints were all-cause death and the combined event of all-cause death or worsening heart failure. Outcomes were assessed by the Kaplan-Meier method and multivariable Cox regression. RESULTS: The prevalence of frailty, based on 4 different criteria, varied from 32.7% to 62.7%. Dependence, depression, nutritional risk, and cognitive impairment were detected in up to 70.9%, 29.1%, 27.3%, and 15.5% of patients, respectively. Frailty, defined as a Clinical Frailty Scale > 4, a Survey of Health, Ageing and Retirement in Europe-Frailty Instrument > 2, or a Short Physical Performance Battery < 10, was independently associated with an increased risk of both study outcomes. Dependence (Katz index < 6) and cognitive impairment (Mini Examen Cognitivo score < 23) were also independent predictors of both outcomes. Frailty diagnosis showed incremental prognostic value when added to United Kingdom National Amyloidosis Centre stages. CONCLUSIONS: Frailty is frequent in patients with ATTR-CM and is associated with impaired clinical outcomes.

title: Cardiac and vascular involvement in protein misfolding diseases
abstract: Protein misfolding diseases impose a substantial and often under-recognized burden on both the heart and vasculature. In this Review, we outline how the failure of proteostasis drives oligomer toxicity, amyloid deposition and inflammation in cardiovascular tissues as well as microvascular injury and thrombosis, which culminate in cardiovascular dysfunction. We define the cardiovascular hallmarks of protein misfolding diseases, focusing on transthyretin amyloidosis and immunoglobulin light chain amyloidosis, and the disease-specific organ tropisms. We examine neurodegenerative proteinopathies affecting the heart-vascular-brain axis, highlighting how amyloid-β and α-synuclein accumulation contribute to dysautonomia, vascular dysfunction and adverse outcomes. We summarize diagnostic pathways and clinical indicators for early diagnosis of cardiovascular involvement in protein misfolding diseases and review established and emerging biomarkers of vascular stress and proteotoxic load. We also map the current therapeutic landscape for protein misfolding diseases, including strategies to reduce the synthesis of precursor proteins or promote the stabilization of mature proteins as well as fibril-directed therapies, and discuss remaining challenges, such as residual cardiovascular risk, that support the development of mechanism-informed therapeutic approaches. Finally, we propose a research roadmap that prioritizes systematic cardiovascular screening in at-risk populations, harmonized methods for vascular phenotyping, biomarker-anchored mechanistic clinical trials across protein misfolding diseases, and artificial intelligence-based approaches and precision medicine frameworks that integrate genotype or distinct protein conformational strain patterns, organ tropism and dynamic proteostasis measures.

title: CT-Based Deep Learning Assessment of Aortic Valve Fibrosis and Calcification: Development and Multicenter External Validation Against Experts, Histology, and Outcomes
abstract: BACKGROUND: Computed tomography angiography (CTA) enables assessment of aortic valve tissue composition, providing insights into disease progression and helping predict outcomes in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement for severe aortic stenosis (AS). The authors aimed to develop a deep learning system for CTA-based quantification of aortic fibrotic and calcific tissue, validate its agreement with expert manual analysis and histopathology, and evaluate its value for outcome prediction. METHODS: This international, multicenter study included 1,674 patients who underwent CTA at 9 sites. A deep learning model based on the nnU-Net architecture was trained in 468 patients and applied to an external test set of 1,206 patients, including 29 with valve histology and 12 with serial CTA. In 1,165 patients with clinical outcomes, prognostic value was assessed adjusting for clinical, echocardiographic, and procedural covariates. RESULTS: Deep learning-enabled tissue composition analysis was rapid (1.35 ± 0.4 min vs 7.2 ± 1.2 min for experts) with excellent agreement vs expert assessment (r = 0.915; intraclass correlation coefficient [ICC] = 0.913), histology (r = 0.909; ICC = 0.905), and scan-rescan reproducibility (r = 0.999; ICC = 0.999). In the external cohort, 469 patients (40%) died over 4.1 ± 1.1 years of follow-up. Fibrotic tissue volume (adjusted HR [aHR] 1.42 per IQR increase; P < 0.001), calcific tissue attenuation (aHR 1.02 per 25 HU increase; P = 0.005), left ventricular ejection fraction (aHR 1.10 per 5% decrease; P < 0.001), life-threatening bleeding (aHR: 1.96; P = 0.003), major vascular complication (aHR: 1.51; P = 0.042) and postprocedural peak pressure gradient (aHR 1.03 per 1 mm Hg increase; P < 0.001) independently predicted mortality. Patients in the highest tertile of fibrotic tissue volume (>0.940 cm3) had a 2-fold higher risk of death (aHR: 2.0; P < 0.001), whereas patients with dense calcific tissue attenuation (>885 HU) had a 1.5-fold higher risk of death. CONCLUSIONS: Deep learning enables rapid quantification of aortic valve fibrotic and calcific tissue from CTA, demonstrating excellent agreement with both expert CTA and histological assessments. Quantitative analysis of aortic tissue composition provides additional prognostic value for all-cause mortality after transcatheter aortic valve replacement in multicenter external evaluation.

title: Impact of CKD and Hemodialysis on Treatment of Severely Calcified Lesions: The ECLIPSE Trial
abstract: Background: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) and coronary calcification increase risk for adverse events following drug-eluting stent (DES) implantation. We evaluated whether outcomes following vessel preparation with orbital atherectomy (OA) versus balloon angioplasty (BA) vary according to CKD. Methods: This pre-specified CKD sub-analysis of the prospective, multicenter ECLIPSE trial evaluated 2,001 patients with severely calcified lesions randomized to OA versus BA prior to DES. Independent predictors of two-year target-vessel failure (TVF)-a composite of cardiac death, target-vessel myocardial infarction (TV-MI), or ischemia-driven target-vessel revascularization (ID-TVR)-were determined using multivariable Cox proportional hazards modeling. Results: CKD (eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² or hemodialysis) was present in 694 (34.7%) patients; 112 required hemodialysis. Two-year TVF was significantly higher with versus without CKD (21.2% vs. 11.6%; p<0.001), driven by increased cardiac death and ID-TVR. Hemodialysis independently predicted TVF (adjusted HR 2.14, 95% CI 1.30-3.53; p=0.003), whereas reduced eGFR alone did not (p=0.070). In patients on hemodialysis, OA versus BA was associated with higher rates of TVF (52.3% vs. 30.7%; adjusted HR 2.50, 95% CI 1.16-5.41; P=0.020), driven by higher rates of TV-MI and ID-TVR, whereas TVF was similar after OA versus BA in patients not on hemodialysis (13.5% vs. 13.1%; adjusted HR 1.05, 95% CI 0.81-1.35; P=0.730); however, the interaction between treatment assignment and hemodialysis status was not significant (Pint=0.244). Conclusions: CKD remains a major predictor of adverse outcomes after DES implantation in severely calcified lesions, with the highest risks in patients on hemodialysis. In the ECLIPSE trial, higher two-year rates of TVF were observed after vessel preparation with OA compared with BA in patients on hemodialysis but not in patients with CKD not on hemodialysis or in those without CKD. Given the modest hemodialysis subgroup size and non-significant interaction testing, confirmation of these findings in additional studies is warranted.
